paper_title: Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own code and checking each version with executable tests. Bringing these mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them. We examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves. Gains carry forward only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change the improver's knowledge or tools, but the physical studies reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion. We synthesize these findings into evaluation principles and research directions for machines that, trial by trial, safely improve the way they improve.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: 1 / Introduction Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes system that improves the process by which it improves, not only its behavior. The idea goes back to I. J. Goods speculation about machines that design better machines (Good, 1966) and to self-referential learners such as the Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2003), and recent digital agents have begun to approach it (Chen et al., 2026d). STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024) applies program that improves code to its own source, and the Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2026c) lets improved coding agents modify themselves; both judge each candidate with executable tests. Yet system can get better at task, and fixed procedure can keep producing better versions of it, without anything recursive happening. RSI requires two further links (Section 2.2): what the system retains from earlier improvements must make its next revision better, and the improver, the component that revises the learning procedure, must in turn use what it has gained to help produce its own next improvement. Physical RSI asks the same question of systems that learn by acting in the physical world, such as robots. Digital RSI supplies the mechanisms (language models that write reward code or controllers, archives of earlier variants, and automated experiment loops); physical RSI tests how these mechanisms use physical experience and whether they hold under physical constraints (Figure 1). The physical setting changes the experimental conditions in four ways  (Table 1)  . First, physical outcome checks depend on sensors and task-specific verifiers, people, or learned detectors whose reliability must be established; even an automated grasp-success check can miss what it does not sense, and an error in that judgment can be reinforced and then executed on hardware. Second, every candidate costs robot time, resets, supervision, and wear, so revision must pay off within few trials. Third, practice changes its own conditions: objects move, grippers wear, calibration drifts, and rolling back software does not repair damaged object. Fourth, what can be improved extends beyond prompts and code to controllers, dynamics models, and the interface to particular body. Each difference bears on the central question of RSI, whether what one round of revision teaches the improver makes the next revision better. Table 1. sections.title: Scoring errors can reinforce faulty actions
sections.content: Consider robot arm that keeps missing the same grasp. The failure can have several causes, and each calls for change kept in different place; these places organize Sections 3.1 and 3.2. The robots policy, the learned controller that turns observations into motor commands, may never produce the recovery motion; an expert correction can teach it, as RECAP (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026) learns from deployment experience and corrections (Section 3.1.1). The robot may mistake light touch for stable hold because its model of contact is wrong; world model refitted to contact data can correct the prediction and give the policy place to practice, as in PlayWorld (Yin et al., 2026b) (Section 3.1.2). The robot may have recovered from this failure before without keeping what worked; external knowledge, such as saved recovery or program, can be called the next time, as Zetta (Ding et al., 2026) grows code-based critics and recoveries 3 PhysicalRSI 1 / Introduction around frozen policy in simulation (Section 3.1.3). Finally, the robot may keep choosing the wrong kind of repair; then the learning procedure must change: which attempts to collect, how to judge them, and how to turn them into updates (Section 3.2). Eureka (Ma et al., 2024a) rewrites reward code from simulated training results, and ENPIRE (Xiao et al., 2026b) lets coding agents modify the training infrastructure from robot experiments. The first three routes improve what the robot does; the fourth improves how it learns, and it is where physical RSI would begin. Recursion would further require that knowledge of why earlier repairs worked, which we call repair knowledge, improves how the next procedure revision is made. Figure 2 contrasts this route with applying fixed training recipe to new experience. Our central argument is that physical experience can improve task competence, the learning procedure, and the improver that revises this procedure, and that four recurring conditions, each sharpened by the physical setting, decide whether such gains carry forward. Each can fail: the new signal may not address what the learner still lacks, because sensing shows only part of failure; the receiving component may be unable to absorb it on its body; its value may not survive later changes in behavior or hardware; or further practice may become unsafe or unaffordable. For the grasping robot, this could mean collecting more of the grasps it already makes well, refining contact model that its controller cannot use, relying on fix that stops working once the gripper is replaced, or practicing until the gripper wears out. change can improve execution and still fail to help later learning: added autonomous data often yield modest gains that saturate and can even regress (Mirchandani et al., 2025). Several research traditions supply From learning actions to improving how learning happens. pieces of this progression. Self-supervised grasping showed that physical outcomes alone can supervise behavior at scale, first by learning from tens of thousands of real grasp attempts (Pinto and Gupta, 2016) and then through large-scale real-robot reinforcement learning (RL) with QT-Opt (Kalashnikov et al., 2018). Interactive imitation learning, as in DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) and HG-DAgger (Kelly et al., 2019), showed how an expert can correct the learner in the states that the learner itself reaches. Lifelong robot learning (Thrun and Mitchell, 1995) asks how knowledge gained on earlier tasks can reduce the real-world experimentation needed for later ones; model-based RL, from Dyna (Sutton, 1990) and PILCO (Deisenroth and Rasmussen, 2011) to Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2020), asks how recorded transitions can support practice inside learned model; and skill-based approaches, such as options (Sutton et al., 1999) and the shared RoboEarth knowledge base (Waibel et al., 2011), ask how an extended behavior can be stored and called again. Each tradition widened what one learning episode can pass on to the next. Recent generalist and foundation-model-based systems widen both what can change and what role the change plays. RoboCat (Bousmalis et al., 2024) turns policy adapted to new task into source of training data for the next generalist, and SILVR (Luo et al., 2026a) revises video-based planner using its own executions. In RoboCat, Eureka (in simulation), and ENPIRE, experience reaches the machinery that produces future updates (a data collector, reward function, the training infrastructure) as well as the policy that receives them. This brings the physical problem close to the long-standing aspiration of learning to learn (Thrun and Pratt, 1998), and several reviewed systems already contain the components that demonstration of recursion would need. The open question is how to realize that aspiration with limited trials, imperfect sensing, and body that changes over time. Scope and related surveys. Our scope is the improvement of policies, world models, memories, skills, and the software procedures that update or use them, whenever their evidence or evaluation is connected to physical action. We discuss hardware change when it affects compatibility, maintenance, or continued experimentation. Autonomous morphology design and physical self-reconstruction are adjacent topics outside our scope. Recent surveys cover neighboring ground  (Table 2)  . Component names alone cannot answer it, because two data collectors with similar task success can yield training data of very different value; more accurate predictor can still produce less useful training data for policy; and the same kind of retrieved memory can change either how program is repaired or how an outcome is judged. The review makes three connected contributions. First, it positions RSI within robot learning by separating method paradigms and problem settings (from reinforcement learning and meta-learning to AutoML) from ladder of claims (behavioral improvement, later-learning benefit, procedure improvement, and the two links of recursion), each defined by the comparison that would establish it. sections.title: 2 Foundations of Physical RSI
sections.content: We follow every system in this review along one path: from experience, to retained change, to the changes next use. Later sections use this path to work out when gain survives another round, without assuming common architecture.

sections.title: 2.1 Learning to Act
sections.content: A few groups of ideas are enough to follow the rest of the review. We introduce them with the running example of the robot that keeps missing grasp. Policies. policy is the controller that maps what the robot currently observes (camera images, joint angles, force readings, and possibly language instruction) to its next motor command; for the grasping robot, it turns view of the object into the next movement of the arm and gripper. In the systems reviewed here, policies are usually neural networks. Generalist policies are trained on large collections of robot data spanning many tasks, as in RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2023b), and sometimes many robot bodies, or embodiments, as in Octo (Octo Model Team et al., 2024). vision-language model (VLM) reads images and text and outputs text; robot systems often use one to propose goals or to judge whether an attempt succeeded. vision-language-action (VLA) model is generalist policy built on pretrained VLM, so that it reads images and an instruction and outputs actions; RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023a), OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), and 𝜋0 (Black et al., 2025) are examples. Many recent policies output short sequence of future actions at once, called an action chunk. Learning from demonstrations. The simplest way to obtain policy is imitation learning from demonstrations, which are often recorded while person teleoperates the robot (Argall et al., 2009). In behavior cloning (BC), the policy is trained to reproduce the demonstrated action in each recorded situation. BC learns only from recorded situations, so its small errors can compound: if the gripper drifts slightly off the object into state that no demonstration covers, the policy may have no good action to take. In practice, person often takes over when the robot errs, and these interventions supply corrective training data. In reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton and Barto, 2018; Kober et al., 2013), the Learning from rewards. robot instead tries actions and receives reward that scores the outcome, for example 1 for stable grasp and 0 otherwise. On real robot, rewards do not arrive automatically: person, hand-written check, or learned reward model, such as success detector, must judge each attempt. We call component that supplies such judgments for learning an evaluator. Because rewards are often sparse and delayed, many methods learn value function, or critic, that predicts how much future reward to expect; some systems use the word critic more loosely for any component, learned or hand-written, that scores behavior. The advantage of an action measures how much better it is than what the policy would typically do in the same situation. Off-policy methods can learn from experience collected by earlier versions of the policy or by other sources, which they keep in replay buffer. On hardware, every trial costs time, supervision, wear, and reset that returns the scene to usable starting state, so the source of the reward and the number of available trials become central resources. Improving an existing policy. Large pretrained policies are rarely retrained from scratch. They are fine-tuned, or post-trained, on new data. small residual policy can add corrections on top of the actions of frozen base policy, such as slight change to the angle at which the gripper approaches the object. Distillation trains one policy to imitate another, for example to fold specialists behavior back into generalist. When policy learns sequence of tasks, it can forget earlier ones, problem studied in continual learning (Parisi et al., 2019); replaying stored data from earlier tasks is common protection. Models of the world. world model, or dynamics model, predicts what will happen after an action, for instance the next camera image or the next object positions (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2020). The grasping robots contact model is one example: it predicts whether touch will become stable hold. robot can use such model to plan, by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions, or to generate imagined experience on which policy is trained. physics simulator is hand-built model of this kind; learned world model is fitted to recorded robot data and can be wrong in ways that policy may learn to exploit. Improvements outside the weights. Not every improvement is stored in network weights. system can keep memories of earlier episodes, maintain library of callable skills (Sutton et al., 1999), or write programs that compose perception and control functions (Liang et al., 2023). Large language models are increasingly used to write such code or to revise reward functions (Ma et al., 2024a). Simulation and hardware. Results come either from simulation benchmarks or from hardware experiments on physical robots, and training in simulation before deployment on hardware is called sim-to-real transfer. Section 2.4 discusses what each setting can establish.

sections.title: 2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement
sections.content: Where experience leaves change. We consider loops in which experience produces retained change that affects later attempts or learning. Human demonstration, correction, reset, or approval can remain part of the loop: automation concerns who makes each decision, whereas learning concerns whether experience changes it (Table 17 in Appendix A). failed update can also be informative by showing where this connection breaks. Generic pretraining without subsequent experienceupdateuse comparison serves as background, as does adaptation confined to single attempt. Rapid Motor Adaptation (Kumar et al., 2021), for example, 8 PhysicalRSI 2 / Foundations of Physical RSI infers current conditions from recent history without retaining the adaptation. Zevas interaction memory is boundary case: it carries across retries within an episode but not across episodes or learning rounds. Simulation-only and formal studies supply enabling mechanisms, while meta-learning, AutoML, and digital agents supply precedents (Section 2.3); direct evidence about physical RSI must come from physical systems. retained change can serve four uses (Figure 4). It can choose or execute actions, predict outcomes or supply practice, support reuse (for example, calling saved recovery or consulting guidance for new program), or change how later data are collected, judged, and turned into updates. These uses are usually carried by policies, world models, external knowledge, and learning procedures, respectively (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). They can overlap: policy can collect training data, model can judge outcomes, and memory can guide an updater. Each study is discussed mainly under the use its experiment tests, regardless of whether its authors call it self-evolving or recursively self-improving. Learner, learning procedure, and improver. The learner acquires task capabilities; the learning procedure determines what experience to collect, how to judge it, and how to construct updates. An improver proposes or selects revisions of that procedure. It may be person, fixed rule, search process, or learned component, with knowledge in memory, weights, code, or prompts. Figure 2 separates the two levels: the learner improves under fixed recipe, whereas the improver revises the recipe itself. In the grasp example, adding corrected grasp to the training data is repair, an update made in response to an observed failure or limitation. The rule choosing which failed grasps need correction belongs to the learning procedure; whoever devises or changes that rule is the improver. The object being changed determines the role: an editor of task skills or data belongs to the procedure, whereas an editor of rewards, evaluators, collection rules, or update-generating training code acts as an improver. From better behavior to recursion. We distinguish four claims  (Table 3)  , and evidence for an earlier claim does not establish later one. Behavioral improvement means better execution under common task test. later-learning benefit means that retained data, weights, models, skills, or code help subsequent learner. Procedure improvement means that revised collector, evaluator, editor, or updater teaches better than its earlier version. This comparison requires matched learners, which differ only in the component under test and share starting conditions, resources, and evaluation protocol (Figure 8). We operationalize recursive self-improvement through two further links, which this review uses as empirical criteria for attributing gain to recursion. First (R1), repair knowledge retained from earlier repairs must improve the improver: on new failures, its procedures must teach matched learners better than those produced by its earlier version. Second (R2), the improver, once improved, must help produce its own next improvement: given the same new repair histories, self-revision proposed using its acquired knowledge must yield an improver that outperforms both the improver it revised and revision of that same improver proposed with the acquired knowledge frozen. fixed improver can repeatedly improve procedures without satisfying either link; an external designers growing expertise does not establish system-level recursion either. Section 3.3 develops the grasp example. concurrent survey grades physical RSI by whether an update changes capabilities or the improvement procedure and whether its gain holds on the same or on other tasks, reserving its top level for an independently verified recursive gain (Zhou et al., 2026a); the claims here are instead defined by the comparison that would establish each. The name is shared by other concurrent work. PhysRSI-eval (Li et al., 2026j) applies it to agents with frozen weights that revise code, tools, and notes after each graded attempt, and Physical RSI 1.0 (MMLab & PhysicalRSI contributors, 2026) names system in which multimodal foundation model revises the harness through which robot acts. We read these works, like any other, by the comparisons they report; name does not establish either link. sections.title: 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning
sections.content: Reinforcement learning and meta-learning already let robots improve from experience and learn how to learn. Self-training, continual learning, and automated machine learning (AutoML) let systems learn from their own outputs, keep learning across tasks, or search for better training recipes. It is therefore fair to ask what RSI adds. These are method paradigms or problem settings, which say how an update is computed or what it must cope with, whereas the claims of Section 2.2 say what an experiment shows to have changed. An RSI system may use any of them to revise any of its components, so the categories overlap rather than exclude one another: RSI is not further paradigm after meta-learning but level of improvement that system built with any of them might reach  (Table 4)  . Standard RL improves policy under an objective and update mechanism Reinforcement learning. chosen before training (Sutton and Barto, 2018). Run repeatedly on hardware, as in HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2025) and RECAP (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026), it yields behavioral improvement, and its data or policy can supply later-learning benefit. RL loops can also be nested inside an outer optimization over part of the learning procedure. Eureka searches over reward programs using the RL training results they produce (Ma et al., 2024a), and meta-gradient RL adapts the return while the agent learns (Xu et al., 2018). LPG discovers an update rule (Oh et al., 2020), and DiscoRL learns such rule across many agents and environments and applies it to unseen benchmarks (Oh et al., 2025). These loops target 11 PhysicalRSI 2 / Foundations of Physical RSI Table 4. How learning paradigms and problem settings relate to the claims of Section 2.2. DERL (Cheng et al., 2025) departs from this on text-based and mathematical reasoning tasks: it trains its reward proposer by policy gradient on the validation success of the inner policies, so the search learns from its own trials, while the rule that trains the proposer stays fixed. In the grasp example, RL that tunes the grasp under fixed slip penalty improves behavior, whereas search that revises the slip penalty changes the procedure; further rounds of the first kind do not become the second. Self-training. Many systems called self-improving train on their own outputs. In self-training such as Noisy Student (Xie et al., 2020), teacher trained on labeled data labels unlabeled data, and student trained on both becomes the next teacher. Expert Iteration (Anthony et al., 2017) and STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) apply the same pattern to search and reasoning, and RoboCat (Bousmalis et al., 2024) applies it to robot data collection. Each round improves behavior and helps the next learner through the data it generates, while the recipe that generates, labels or filters, and trains on the data stays fixed. When the model also judges its own outputs, as in Self-Rewarding Language Models (Yuan et al., 2024), the evaluator changes with training, but the judging prompt and the training recipe do not. Continual learning. Continual, or lifelong, learning asks how learner that meets sequence of tasks can reuse what it learned on earlier ones (Thrun and Mitchell, 1995) without forgetting them (Parisi et al., 2019). Backward and forward transfer (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017) measure how learning one task changes performance on earlier and later ones. Backward transfer thus measures retention, whereas forward transfer as defined there is performance on new task before training on it; LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a), benchmark of sequential robot manipulation tasks, instead scores forward transfer by success on each new task averaged over its training, which is closer to later-learning benefit. Replay, regularization, and other protections against forgetting are usually chosen by designers, so continual learning defines setting that an RSI system must also handle (Section 4.2) rather than way of improving the improver. Meta-learning. Meta-learning trains over many tasks so that new tasks are learned faster (Thrun and Pratt, 1998), and what it learns decides which claim it can support. An initialization from which few gradient steps solve new task, as in MAML (Finn et al., 2017), is an acquired artifact and supports later-learning benefit. Other methods learn part of the learning procedure: recurrent policies whose activations carry out adaptation (Duan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016), dynamics prior that adapts online, 12 PhysicalRSI 2 / Foundations of Physical RSI as in GrBAL (Nagabandi et al., 2019), learned optimizers (Andrychowicz et al., 2016), and evolved or learned losses (Houthooft et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2018; Bechtle et al., 2021). When learner guided by such part learns better than matched learner guided by the original, the comparison supports procedure improvement. LMPC (Liang et al., 2024) is boundary case: it fine-tunes the model that writes reward code on past teaching sessions so that later teaching needs fewer turns, but that code drives model-predictive controller directly rather than training run, so the gain lies in how behavior is constructed. The outer meta-training procedure that produces the part (a gradient loop, an evolutionary search, or fine-tuning recipe) is specified by its designers and is not changed by the revisions it produces, so learning reaches the procedure but not the process that produces it. Automated machine learning. AutoML searches over architectures, hyperparameters, and training pipelines (Hutter et al., 2019), and AutoML-Zero extends the search to learning algorithms (Real et al., 2020); found configuration that teaches matched learners better supports procedure improvement. Some searchers learn from their own record: the controller of neural architecture search (Zoph and Le, 2017) is trained with reinforcement learning on the validation accuracy of the architectures it generates. Because it edits the learner rather than the rules for collecting, judging, or updating, it is learned part of the procedure, like the skill editor of PRACTICE (Bai et al., 2026), and the rule that trains it stays fixed. Where recursion adds requirement. RSI moves the process that produces revisions inside as well, as the two links of Section 2.2 require. The requirement is self-referential, as in the Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2003), STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024), the Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2026c), and Gödel Agent (Yin et al., 2025), which let the improving process act on its own code. Generalized Agent Iteration places iterative policy improvement and RSI in one formal framework, in which whether the improvement mechanism sits inside the agent separates the two, and whether the evaluation standard is grounded outside it decides whether goals can drift (Tang et al., 2026). The criterion is therefore which component changes with the revision history, not whether some outer recipe stays fixed. In the metalearning and AutoML methods above, the component that produces revisions of the learning procedure does not change; an improver fine-tuned by fixed recipe on its own repair histories does change and can satisfy R1, which the frozen-knowledge comparison of Section 4.4 tests. Conversely, an improver whose code changes in every round satisfies neither link if the changes come from designer or from search that learns nothing from earlier rounds.

sections.title: 2.4 Facing Physical Limits
sections.content: Table 1 lists the terms we use to judge how closely study is tied to physical experience. Hardware interaction connects learning directly to physical consequences, but consequence still needs diagnosis and reliable judge. binary failure label on grasp may not distinguish pose error from slip, whereas force measurements or contact history may separate the two. Simulation, learned prediction, and formal checks represent selected consequences whose adequacy must be tested at the decision they support. Simulation is cheap and repeatable but omits some physical effects, whereas hardware captures real contact, sensing, and wear but allows few trials, so the two settings support different conclusions about cost, transfer, and the comparisons study can afford. Because practice changes its own conditions (Section 1), returning to usable starting state may require reset policy or human assistance; early work on autonomous real-world RL already named resets, onboard perception, and rewards without instrumentation as the ingredients that continued learning needs (Zhu et al., 2020). Moving knowledge to another robot adds further gap, because reuse across bodies needs compatible coordinates, timing, sensing, and reachable effects. studys connection to physical experience is therefore matter of degree. It depends on the success evaluation (who or what judges whether an attempt succeeded), on interaction coverage and recoverability, and on whether successive trials remain 13 PhysicalRSI 2 / Foundations of Physical RSI comparable. The success evaluation may rely on the same evaluator that supplied the learning signal or on one independent of it, difference that Section 4.1 shows to matter. Table 1 contrasts these conditions with those of digital self-improvement, Section 4.3 develops their consequences for continued learning, and Table 18 in Appendix shows what evidence each robot domain contributes. These conditions weigh on each paradigm of Section 2.3 in different place. Meta-learning needs distribution of training tasks, and on hardware every sampled task costs trials, resets, and supervision; domain-adaptive meta-learning meta-trains on previously collected human and robot demonstrations, and LMPC collected its training data in simulation. Eureka and DrEureka run their reward search in simulation, where many candidates can be trained in parallel, and DrEureka then deploys the resulting policy on hardware (Ma et al., 2024b). For RSI, the bottleneck shifts to revision histories: an improver learns from them, and each entry needs at least one learning round judged by physical trials, so these histories accumulate more slowly than the task samples of meta-learning or the transitions of RL, and no executable test settles whether revision helped. Simulation, stored traces, and learned models can screen candidate revisions before hardware trials, but their adequacy for that screening is itself claim to test (Section 4.4).

sections.title: 2.5 Benchmarking Self-Improvement
sections.content: Most comparisons in this review run in simulation, and the benchmarks differ in what they stress  (Table 5)  . LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a) supplies sequential manipulation suites, and LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025b) perturbs manipulated objects, initial states, task instructions, and environments to test whether behavior depends on the original cues; LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) varies seven factors, including camera viewpoint, initial robot state, and sensor noise. RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) broadens household task coverage, and RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025c) and RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026g) cover bimanual manipulation. VLABench (Zhang et al., 2025d) and Meta-World (Yu et al., 2019) supply further manipulation suites, and SIMPLER (Li et al., 2024) mirrors real robot setups for policy evaluation. Navigation studies use Habitat (Savva et al., 2019) and R2R-CE (Krantz et al., 2020), and household agents use EmbodiedBench (Yang et al., 2025). Except for LIBEROs lifelong protocol, which scores transfer and forgetting along task sequence, these suites test system at one point in time, and claim about improvement across rounds still needs protocol on top that fixes what carries over between rounds and what stays held out (Section 4.2). recent benchmark prototype moves in this direction: it provides no in-domain demonstrations, carries experience over between requests within deployment, and names how quickly an agent becomes competent in deployment as quantity of interest (Cai et al., 2026). PhysRSI-eval (Li et al., 2026j) fixes what carries over between rounds, in simulation. Six model-and-configuration systems revise persistent workspace of code, tools and notes with frozen weights, for up to 17 graded rounds on each of 18 RoboDojo tasks, and each system is scored on five axes: first-attempt score, how early gains appear, attained score, physical budget saved, and the share of first-round failures later solved. The axes need not agree: Claude Opus 5.5 attains higher score than GPT-6.1 Sol but scores lower on gain timing and budget saved. In six-task ablation with GPT-6 Astra, withholding all information from earlier rounds lowers success over rounds 46 from 15 of 36 attempts to 3 of 36. second group of benchmarks targets the components on which self-improvement relies. FailBench (Navasardyan et al., 2026) tests success detectors on 2,197 real and simulated manipulation attempts, where the best of 13 VLM detectors reaches 0.77 balanced accuracy. CaliBench (Sadeghi et al., 2026) tests whether the outcome frequencies of video world models are calibrated. MC-EvoBench (Song et al., 2026a) fixes the controls that transfer claim needs, and RLE-Bench (Ma et al., 2026) holds out robustness perturbations that coding agents cannot query. RoboCoach-Bench (Lei et al., 2026) collects 32 simulated tasks for agents that write and revise training code. Digital benchmarks of recursive self-improvement isolate related questions. Hardware evaluations instead use task suites built by each study, and their budgets vary widely, from handful of trials per task, as in PhysEvos 25 trials over five real tasks (Tian et al., 2026), to hundreds of evaluation episodes, as in the more than 600 pairwise episodes of RoboArena (Atreya et al., 2025). Most controlled downstream comparisons concern manipulation; navigation, locomotion, flight, and robotic laboratories support particular mechanisms without testing each condition across robot bodies  (Table 18)  . Simulation results support mechanism comparisons at scale, whereas hardware results show what survives real contact, sensing, and resets (Section 2.4). Because tasks, trial counts, and metrics differ, results are compared within each study rather than across studies; Appendix records the settings behind selected numbers. Most studies report success rate, the fraction of trials that reach task-defined goal as judged by person, scripted check, or learned detector. Some give partial credit for progress through task stages, 15 PhysicalRSI 3 / Mechanisms toward Physical RSI which needs different statistical model than binary success. Others add efficiency during execution, such as cycle time in HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2025) or throughput in RECAP (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026). Learning efficiency is reported as the time, episodes, or supervision needed to reach level of performance. ConRFT (Chen et al., 2025d) reaches 96.3% average success on eight real tasks after 4590 minutes of online fine-tuning, and VLAC (Zhai et al., 2025) raises real success from about 30% to 90% within 200 episodes. ENPIRE (Xiao et al., 2026b) reports the time its robot fleet needs to reach target, and LMPC (Liang et al., 2024) counts chat turns per successful teaching session. Retention asks whether earlier competence survives later learning or deployment, and later-learning benefit on new task is forward transfer. ACCRUE (Kim et al., 2026) reports transfer as cut in real-robot training time for later tasks, CIDER (Li et al., 2026d) reports forward transfer of an accumulated policy, and MC-EvoBench sets out the controls that such claim needs. Resource use is counted in robot hours, demonstrations, interventions, compute, or model tokens. CARD (Sun et al., 2024) needs about 14K tokens per task against about 663K for Eureka, and ENPIREs fleet scaling shortens the time to target at lower per-robot utilization and faster-than-linear token growth; because studies count different parts of this work, their costs are not directly comparable (Section 4.1).

sections.title: 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI
sections.content: This section reviews physical self-improvement by what system actually changes, following the ladder of Section 2.2. Section 3.1 covers changes to the learner 𝐿, kept in policies, world models, or external knowledge; policy trained with relabeled targets, reward, or an optimization algorithm belongs there, because those rules stay fixed. Section 3.2 covers changes to the rules themselves, the learning procedure 𝑃 that collects, judges, and updates, and Section 3.3 covers changes to the improver 𝐼 𝐾 that revises that procedure (notation of Section 2.2). Section 3.4 adds no fourth component: it asks whether these layers close into recursive relation, in which the improver, once improved, helps produce its own next improvement. system that serves several roles is discussed mainly where its experiment tests it, with cross-references elsewhere; Table 11 collects the systems that describe themselves as recursive self-improvement.

sections.title: 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge
sections.content: This section reviews the base loop of physical self-improvement: experience improves what the robot does, and the data, models, and skills it leaves behind can help later learners. These are the first two claims of Section 2.2, behavioral improvement and later-learning benefit. We follow the change to where it is kept, in policy (Section 3.1.1), world model (Section 3.1.2), or memories, skills, and code (Section 3.1.3). The learning procedure that produces these changes stays fixed here; where study also changes how experience is collected, judged, or turned into updates, that part appears in Section 3.2.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Policy Updates
sections.content: The most direct way for experience to help is to change the policy itself, and on the path to RSI the policy is also the most common target of revised learning procedure. deployed policy determines both what the robot does and which situations later appear in its training data, so the question to ask of new data is what learning signal they contain. Four kinds of signal recur. Relabeling reinterprets behavior that has already happened: an attempt that pushed the cup aside instead of grasping it is still correct example of how to push the cup aside. reward scores attempted outcomes so that optimization can prefer better ones. correction supplies an action that the policy did not take, typically from person who intervenes. Replay reuses earlier experience to preserve or recover previously learned behavior (Figure 5). Each column follows the grasp example: what was experienced, what the signal changes in the training data, and representative systems from this section. From practice to training targets. recorded trajectory becomes useful for learning only once goal, reward, or action label is attached to it. Hindsight experience replay (Andrychowicz et al., 2017) relabels an attempt with the goal it actually achieved, and SOAR (Zhou et al., 2025c) carries this achievedgoal relabeling to goal-conditioned imitation. Earlier large-scale systems such as MT-Opt (Kalashnikov et al., 2022) shared physical outcomes across twelve tasks; pretrained generalists change the starting point, because practice can refine behavior that is already useful, and value-based fine-tuning must then keep offline estimates calibrated, as Cal-QL (Nakamoto et al., 2023) does in simulation. RoboCat (Bousmalis et al., 2024) closes the resulting cycle: generalist adapted to target task from demonstrations collects trajectories that, mixed with retained multi-task data, retrain the generalist offline. RoboCat also relabels unsuccessful episodes with the goals they reached, whereas SOAR retrains only on attempts that its fixed VLM judges successful (Appendix B). Adding more of the robots own data does not necessarily improve the targets it learns from. In their study of mostly single-task policies on five simulated and two real manipulation tasks, Mirchandani et al. (2025) find that added autonomous data yield modest gains that saturate and, over two to four collection rounds, can regress. On two of the tasks, human demonstrations started from conditions where rollouts had failed help more than randomly chosen ones, whereas autonomous collection from the same conditions offers no comparable advantage. More state diversity in demonstration data does not always help, whereas inconsistent actions often hurt (Belkhale et al., 2023). These results separate two needs, finding the difficult conditions and supplying useful actions there; repeating the policys familiar successes addresses neither. From feedback to better actions. Relabeling cannot supply an action the policy never produced, but an incomplete attempt can still reveal partial progress, and person can replace part of it with corrective motion. SI-EFM (Ghasemipour et al., 2025) takes the first route: frozen model of the steps remaining to goal rewards each step that brings the robot closer, and policy gradients then learn from incomplete real-robot attempts without new demonstrations, though only among variations that the policy actually tries. FAR (Hao et al., 2026) uses failed attempts in different way: it turns them into preference data that steers retries away from the failed behavior and adds successful recoveries to later training, with gains in simulation and on real manipulation tasks. Corrections take the second route. HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2025) builds on SERL (Luo et al., 2024), which combines off-policy learning, learned reward classifiers, and reset policies, and adds online human interventions so that corrective transitions inform the critic that guides the actor. RECAP (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026) conditions the policy on the advantage of each action, fitted from deployment trajectories and expert corrections. Max-Q selective imitation (Wang and Wang, 2026) regresses the actor toward whichever action Monte Carlo chunk critic scores higher: its own action or replay-buffer action, 17 PhysicalRSI 3 / Mechanisms toward Physical RSI which is often an intervention. The target therefore shifts from corrections to the policys own behavior as it improves. On real USB insertion, it reaches 99% success after half an hour, whereas HIL-SERL needs about five hours to reach its 100% ceiling (each at its best checkpoint). SiLRI (Zhao et al., 2025) treats human interventions as possibly suboptimal: it poses real-world RL as constrained problem whose bound at each state is set by the uncertainty of the interventions, solved with state-wise Lagrange multiplier, and reaches 90% success on real manipulation tasks in at most half the time HIL-SERL needs. The same recorded transition can become value target, weighted action target, or conditioning variable, as RAPolicy (Yang et al., 2026a), SI-EFM, and RECAP illustrate, and which of these the learner receives changes what it learns. Two studies keep pretrained VLA frozen during online learning and train an added module alongside it. BEE (Zhao et al., 2026b) uses the consistency of human corrections to constrain RL updates to residual policy around frozen VLA. On three real tasks and one simulated task, it reaches 91.2% average success against 57.5% for an RL baseline at matched online-data budget. RL Token (Xu et al., 2026b) instead adapts VLA to expose compact readout, keeps it frozen, and trains small actorcritic on that readout online. On four real tasks, minutes to few hours of practice speed up the hardest phase by up to 3 and raise success as judged by human operator, for example from 20% to 65% on screw installation. Outside manipulation, SELFI (Hirose et al., 2024) fine-tunes pretrained navigation policy with online model-free RL whose Q-values keep the model-based objective of its offline pretraining, improving collision avoidance and, in user study, social compliance in real environments. Reward-guided post-training of VLAs has scaled mainly in simulation, while its most reliable results come from smaller hardware studies. VLA-RL (Lu et al., 2025) on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a) and 𝜋RL (Chen et al., 2025b) run in simulation, and FLaRe (Hu et al., 2025a) and SimpleVLA-RL (Li et al., 2026c) add real-robot results. In eight-task hardware studies, ConRFT (Chen et al., 2025d) reaches 96.3% average success after 4590 minutes of online fine-tuning and RL-100 (Lei et al., 2025a) succeeds in 1,000 of 1,000 evaluation episodes. Task-specific hardware studies such as GR-RL (Li et al., 2025b) for shoe lacing and VLA-Precision (Su et al., 2026) for chemistry tasks push precision further (Appendix B). Autonomous real-world RL also reaches beyond tabletop arms: on Spot mobile manipulators, task-relevant autonomy, behavior priors, and generic rewards reach 80% average success on four tasks (Mendonca et al., 2024). Without per-task success checks, such training needs rewards that generalize, and the stricter test of learned reward is the behavior it teaches rather than its prediction accuracy. Pretrained vision and language models supply them as zero-shot similarities in VLM-RM (Rocamonde et al., 2024) and RoboCLIP (Sontakke et al., 2023), both evaluated in simulation, or as embedding distances learned from human video in VIP (Ma et al., 2023b) and LIV (Ma et al., 2023a), both with real-robot evaluations. ReWiND (Zhang et al., 2025c), RoboReward (Lee et al., 2026b), and VLAC (Zhai et al., 2025) judge learned rewards by how they transfer and by the behavior they teach; VLAC raises real success on four tasks from about 30% to 90% within 200 episodes. Finer progress distinctions preserve more of what incomplete attempts teach: SARM2 (Chen et al., 2026e) conditions its reward model on the estimated task stage, adapts it once, and holds it fixed while the SPIRAL loop learns residual corrections to frozen VLA. On crumpled garments, three SPIRAL rounds raise success from 4/12 to 8/12, while the matched loop with only sparse success reward falls from 4/12 to 2/12. Feedback that can rank behavior leaves second choice: where the From proposals to policies. improvement should live. Choosing among proposals can improve execution without retraining, as VGPS (Nakamoto et al., 2024) does by reranking frozen policys proposals with an offline value function; PA-RL (Mark et al., 2024) also improves sampled actions under critic and trains the policy on them with supervised loss. Learned judges can steer frozen policy in the same way. UF-OPS (Attarian et al., 2026) trains success and time-to-success verifiers once on the policys labeled rollouts and selects among sampled action chunks at run time, with reported gains of 25 to 80 percentage points on five real Aloha tasks. World-Coherent Decoding (Zhang et al., 2026b) learns during deployment to rank frozen world action models sampled futures by the mismatch between predicted and observed frames. In 18 PhysicalRSI 3 / Mechanisms toward Physical RSI RoboTwin 2.0 simulation, under the authors limited-randomization protocol, it raises Hard-split success from 55.80% to 60.90%. Keeping scoring, improvement, and policy change separate avoids the need to adapt policy gradients to each action representation, whether iteratively denoised chunks in Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023), discretized tokens in OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), or flow matching in 𝜋0 (Black et al., 2025). Selection gains can stay in the selector or be absorbed into the generator. VERITAS (Zhang and Shah, 2026) behavior-clones trajectories steered toward agreement with visual path proposed by VLM. Q-Planning (Giridhar et al., 2026) instead leaves the cloned policy unchanged and updates Q-function from successful and failed rollouts. On its two real-robot tasks, terminal rewards come from human episode labels and success is measured on the collection episodes themselves. Both routes stay bounded by their proposals: if the generator never produces grasp that avoids the slip, no selector can recover one. residual policy modifies the proposed motion while keeping the base policy as prior. ResiP (Ankile et al., 2025) trains one in simulation and then distills it into vision policy co-trained with real demonstrations. DSRL (Wagenmaker et al., 2025) instead steers the input noise of frozen diffusion policy, searching only within its learned distribution. DPPO (Ren et al., 2025) fine-tunes the diffusion policy itself and transfers simulation-trained assembly policy to hardware. Expanding proposals helps only if the resulting experience teaches the policy where it needs help, which PLD (Xiao et al., 2026a) tests directly. residual-RL specialist takes over after the generalist has run for sampled number of steps, and the hybrid trajectories are distilled back. In real cube pickup, PLD specialist and an RLPD (Ball et al., 2023) specialist both reach full success within two hours from the same initialization, and each supplies 200 successful trajectories to the same distillation. The resulting generalists nevertheless differ, succeeding in 30 and 16 of 30 trials, respectively, because only the PLD data include recoveries from the corner states that the learner itself visits; collector success alone therefore does not reveal training value. Delay creates further mismatch: Real-Time EXPO-FT (Dong et al., 2026) edits the action chunks of slower VLA with the latest observation and selects among candidates with critic, because an action can become wrong between prediction and execution. Selection suffices when useful behavior already lies in the proposal set; otherwise the generator must be optimized, corrected, steered, or fine-tuned, and distillation retains corrections that should become habitual  (Table 6)  . From single runs to lifelong practice. At scale, RoboNet (Dasari et al., 2020) pools trajectories across laboratories and embodiments, and Learning While Deploying (Wang et al., 2026j) repeatedly updates one generalist from rollouts and interventions across sixteen robots. SOP (Pan et al., 2026) streams on-policy experience and human interventions from fleet to cloud learner and reports real-world performance that scales near-linearly with the number of robots. OpenBot-Fleet (Müller et al., 2024) sends learned navigation policies back to user-operated robots. More sources widen coverage only where observations, actions, and task definitions align. Practice also needs way back to useful starting state: Leave No Trace (Eysenbach et al., 2018) learns forward and reset policies in simulation, ReLMM (Sun et al., 2022) learns reset-free on physical mobile manipulator, and MEDAL++ (Sharma et al., 2023) and RoboFuME (Yang et al., 2024a) need only occasional manual resets on real robots. Against forgetting, capacity can be allocated or routed, as AtomicVLA (Zhang et al., 2026g) grows expert modules for atomic skills and CLARE (Römer et al., 2026b) expands and selects adapters without task labels, or adaptation can be combined with rehearsal, as in LifelongVLA (He et al., 2026b) and iManip (Zheng et al., 2025), or with targeted replay, as in Memory Anchors (Du et al., 2026). Separation costs capacity and routing; retaining experience, as in gradient episodic memory (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017), costs storage but can also speed later tasks (Xie and Finn, 2022). CIDER (Li et al., 2026d) freezes the accumulated policy as teacher before each new task and alternates current-task RL with distillation on archived states; over six real tasks and three runs each, the retained policy needs no more training steps to reach the success criterion than the same RL agent from the common initialization, and fewer on some tasks. sections.title: Different failures call for different teaching signals
sections.content: Match the signal to the failure. More successes supply neither missing action nor finer distinction. The signal must reach an executable action. An optimizer, selector, or action interface must absorb it, and changed behavior calls for rechecking coverage, retention, and the interface. Behavioral gains are well established; later-learning benefits are rarer. Hardware comparisons establish behavioral gains; RoboCat, PLD, and CIDER also report later-learning benefits. sections.title: 3.1.2 World Models for Prediction and Practice
sections.content: Physical trials are slow and costly, so natural way to stretch them is to learn model of the world and practice inside it. world model predicts how physical state may change after an action; for grasp, it might predict whether the object will stay between the fingers when the gripper closes. The prediction can serve as plan that must be translated into motion, as imagined experience from which policy is trained, or as predicted features supplied to policy. Each role tests different form of usability: success in one role says little about the others. Generative video models offer all three interfaces: generated video serves as plan in UniPi (Du et al., 2023), as controllable simulator in UniSim (Yang et al., 2024b) and, learned without action labels, in Genie (Bruce et al., 2024), and as policy-training data in DreamGen (Jang et al., 2025). Cosmos (NVIDIA et al., 2025) develops world foundation models for physical applications, WISA (Wang et al., 2025a) and PISA (Li et al., 2025a) target physical consistency, and SPIRAL (Yang et al., 2026d) (unrelated to the SPIRAL policy loop of Section 3.1.1) updates its generator with critic that checks action adherence and physical realism. world model can also enter the learning procedure by judging candidate policies or changes before they reach hardware (Sections 3.2.2 and 4.4). Using models to plan and train. Classical model-based methods supplied the main ingredients. Dyna (Sutton, 1990) interleaves real and modeled experience, PILCO (Deisenroth and Rasmussen, 2011) and PETS (Chua et al., 2018) account for model uncertainty, MBPO (Janner et al., 2019) keeps imagined rollouts short to limit compounding error, self-supervised visual planning (Ebert et al., 2017) plans through learned video prediction, and latent world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2020) train policies in compact dynamics, as DayDreamer (Wu et al., 2023) did on physical robots. models value for control need not track its prediction accuracy (Lambert et al., 2020; Farahmand et al., 2017; Grimm et al., 2020). Planning first exposes an interface problem: predicted video of the gripper closing is not yet robot command. SILVR (Luo et al., 2026a) translates video plans through separately trained inverse-dynamics model, and on hardware its successful executions update only the task video planner. In its simulated MetaWorld (Yu et al., 2019) ablation over twelve unseen tasks, updating both planner and translator reaches 44.2% success, against 26.8% with the translator frozen: an improving planner can be held back by translator that cannot express its new motions. The hardware counterpart of this comparison remains to be run. model used for training shifts the burden to policy optimization, and its gain depends on how far the policy may optimize against the model. RISE (Yang et al., 2026b) freezes its learned dynamics and value models, limits imagined interactions to two steps, and updates an advantage-conditioned VLA; its hardware comparison reimplements RECAP (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026) with the same 𝜋0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) initialization, because the 𝜋0.6 model used by RECAP is not available. PlayWorld (Yin et al., 2026b) trains only the small DSRL (Wagenmaker et al., 2025) policy that chooses its generators input noise against the fitted world model, rewarded by progress estimator trained on demonstrations; with twenty hardware trials per checkpoint, its best reported task improves by 65 percentage points over the base policy, yet later optimization inside the model can reduce real success. WMPO (Zhu et al., 2025b), CtrlWorld (Guo et al., 2025), ProphRL (Zhang et al., 2025b), and World-Gymnast (Sharma et al., 2026) likewise improve VLAs with imagined rollouts. Fine-tuning on imagined successes raises Ctrl-Worlds policy success by 44.7 percentage points, and ProphRL, which runs flow-policy GRPO inside an action-conditioned video model pretrained on more than 31M trajectories, raises overall success on four real UR30e tasks by 24.6 to 30.0 percentage points over the starting policies of three VLA backbones (Appendix B). Whether new physical experience should also repair the practice model is further choice, one that changes what later updates learn from; Section 3.2.3 follows VLAWs loop of this kind. Whether new rollouts can repair model depends on what they cover for the component that consumes them. contact model needs partial contacts, slips, and recoveries, not only successes: PlayWorld collects such evidence through autonomous play, SILVR through task-directed rollouts from its current planner, and Motus2 (Bi et al., 2026) routes curated successes to action generation and failed or suboptimal interactions to dynamics or value prediction, freezing its video backbone and evaluator during later policy optimization. When natural failures miss the needed corrections, XPACE (Wei et al., 2026a) constructs them: its world model renders deviations from expert demonstrations followed by recoveries, and fine-tuning on mixture containing 8% of these examples yields hardware gains across three tasks evaluated with twenty trials per method. failed contact may be valuable for predicting consequences, while only validated recovery should supervise the action policy. Dynamics can also change. Roughly 100 seconds of real quadrotor flight support online identification of residual dynamics model and in-flight policy updates (Ren et al., 2026); Variational Neural Dynamics (Xing et al., 2026) instead infers which recurring operating condition applies from recent interaction; and Selfadapting Robotic Agents (Domberg and Schildbach, 2026) detect out-of-distribution events from prediction residuals and trigger fine-tuning. D-World (Wen and Wang, 2026), which its authors describe as recursive self-improvement, keeps an explicit digital twin that frozen language model revises after each executed action chunk and accepts revision only when replayed residuals do not grow; on real dual-arm robot, one revision reduced rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm. After damage, Bongard et al. (2006) revise model of the robots body and search it for new gait, Intelligent Trial and Error (Cully et al., 2015) searches precomputed repertoire of behaviors, and GrBAL (Nagabandi et al., 2019) adapts meta-learned dynamics prior (Section 2.3). Which route saves physical trials depends on what useful structure survives the change. For control, representation must distinguish futures that imply Shaping what models predict. different actions, which pixel-accurate prediction neither guarantees nor requires. Joint-embedding predictive architectures predict in learned feature spaces and plan toward goals there, as V-JEPA 2AC (Assran et al., 2025) and DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025a) do, and D-JEPA (Liu et al., 2026e) aligns competing predicted futures with the candidate that executes best. Physical properties must remain readable: in PokeWorld (Tan et al., 2026a), predicting touch makes stiffness decodable whereas merely supplying touch as an input does not, and PSG-JEPA (Yan et al., 2026) adds proprioceptive objectives where forward prediction alone omits such structure. DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2025), which reconstructs observations, and TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024), which does not, bracket the design space. Retrieved history in MemWorld (Zheng et al., 2026b), forcetorque prediction in MuSe (Clark et al., 2026), and predicted fingertip wrenches in TORL-VLA (Zheng et al., 2026a) supply distinctions that camera data alone can miss. The information must also reach the policy through usable interface, and the model must respond correctly to commands. GigaBrain-0.5M* (GigaBrain Team et al., 2026) conditions action learning on predicted future-state tokens, whereas VLAW turns predicted futures into reward-filtered training data; conditioned policy may ignore or over-rely on auxiliary tokens, whereas synthetic data may amplify prediction errors. WorldEcho (Chen et al., 2026f) shows that models trained only on expert trajectories, given commands outside that distribution, either ignore the commanded motion or produce visually invalid rollouts, and CausalWorld (Ahmed et al., 2021) lets physical and visual variables be changed independently. Across embodiments, particle-based action representations (He et al., 2026c) offer shared geometric interface, while XEWorld (Chen et al., 2026i) finds that current models bind joint commands more readily to familiar appearance than to transferable kinematics. visually plausible model may still lack decision-relevant state, usable interface, or correct responses to intervention. Failure can enter at four links between model and its policy: transition Judging models by their use. prediction, outcome scoring, policy optimization, or translation into executable motion. End-to-end hardware results, as in RISE and PlayWorld, measure joint usefulness but do not say which link broke, 23 PhysicalRSI 3 / Mechanisms toward Physical RSI so evaluation needs both final performance and comparisons that change one link at time. DexTouchWM (Qin et al., 2026) shows why. Its world model trained on mixed human and robot data improves held-out prediction and, on average, agreement between policy rankings in imagination and on hardware, yet replacing 100 of 200 real training trajectories with synthetic counterparts generated by this model lowers the mean physical partial-credit score for each of three policy families (FTP-1, 𝜋0.5, and X-VLA) across four tasks. model can become better surrogate evaluator and still produce worse training mixture. Other methods change how predictions are consumed. WISE (Zhang et al., 2026a) calls frozen world model only at states where interaction matters and bounds the imagined horizon, and HaWMPO (Chen et al., 2026j) trains hallucination estimator on discrepancies between generated and observed outcomes and uses it to soften rewards from unreliable action chunks. How prediction is queried also matters: in CaliBench (Sadeghi et al., 2026), individually plausible videos can have poorly calibrated outcome frequencies, and in simulated differential-drive study (Raghavan and Singh, 2026), 20-step rollout without intermediate measurements picks different state estimator than closed-loop tracking in 18 of 24 sensing conditions, whereas replay error under the recorded schedule disagrees in five. Evaluation should reproduce the actions, horizon, and observation schedule of the policys use. Synthesis

sections.title: A useful model preserves distinctions the controller can exploit
sections.content: Cover and preserve what the decision requires. Physical data must reach the transitions, contacts, and recoveries the consumer lacks, and prediction must preserve distinctions that change outcomes. Prediction helps only through its consumer. Predictive gains help control only through suitable evaluator, learner, and action interface. Value belongs to the full chain. Hardware gains such as VLAWs belong to combined pipelines, and DexTouch-WMs better surrogate evaluator yields worse training data. Let outcomes select the repair. Refitting the model, restricting imagination, and downweighting unreliable predictions each sit in different system; Section 4.4 asks how physical outcomes could choose among them.

sections.title: 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes
sections.content: Not every useful change needs to enter policys weights or world model. robot that misses grasps might remember that particular object tends to slip, save regrasp routine that worked, or add monitor that interrupts the policy when slip is detected. We use memory for stored information that must be interpreted when it is used, skill for callable behavior with an execution interface, and runtime or software for the logic that retrieves, composes, monitors, or repairs those behaviors (Figure 7). The same artifact can cross these boundaries (a recovery written down as text becomes skill once controller can execute it), but the distinction identifies who uses the change next; for all three, the question is whether change kept outside model weights is usable. On the path to RSI, external knowledge is also where system can keep the repair knowledge that recursion requires (Section 2.2). Earlier systems kept different kinds of artifacts. Options (Sutton et al., 1999) encode temporally extended behaviors that higher-level controller can call, and Horde (Sutton et al., 2011) learns many sensorimotor predictions in parallel. RoboEarth (Waibel et al., 2011) shares models and action recipes among robots. Code as Policies (Liang et al., 2023) writes programs against perception and control APIs, and Inner Monologue (Huang et al., 2023) feeds execution feedback back into planning. In digital environments, including games (Luo et al., 2026b), Voyager (Wang et al., 2024a) accumulates executable skills and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) stores written reflections on earlier failures, showing how frozen model can still take part in an agent that improves; the Weights or Skills? survey (Jena et al., 2026) reviews this broader choice. Each panel shows one saved form of the slip repair and representative systems from this section; reuse on another robot first checks the interface. Remembering experience. Memory systems differ in what they store, how strongly they abstract it, through which interface it is read, and how long it persists, and memory helps only if these choices preserve relation that later decision can exploit. Some systems keep the scene and past interaction themselves: RoboMemory (Lei et al., 2025b) and AllDayNav (Yin et al., 2026a) preserve continuity of the environment and of past interaction, and PhyAgentOS (Liu et al., 2026h) keeps sessions, evidence, recovered lessons, and capability descriptions as versioned records inside runtime that also checks compatibility, supervises execution, and invokes recovery, so its gains belong to the integrated package. Others distill experience into reusable guidance, which must then be checked against later conditions. Robo-Cortex (Chan et al., 2026) distills progress and failure histories into principles and induced navigation heuristics, evaluated mainly in unseen settings of the Habitat simulator (Savva et al., 2019) with preliminary physical study of ten navigation goals. RoboHarn-Evo (Bao et al., 2026) also revises what it stores: physical feedback updates taskand action-level entries together with their stated applicability, and knowledge acquired in simulation reaches 41.7% mean zero-shot success on real tasks, rising to 62.5% after updates from real interaction. PhysMem (Li et al., 2026b) makes the check explicit: frozen VLM planner commits hypothesis about physical properties to memory only after targeted interaction verifies it. On simulated medium-difficulty brick insertion this reaches 76% success against 53% without memory and 23% when raw experience is retrieved directly (100 episodes per condition, three seeds), so retrieving raw experience can do worse than having no memory; its real xArm6 experiments report plan quality over 30-minute deployment sessions. PragmaBot (Qu et al., 2025) summarizes the successful episodes of real legged manipulator into retrievable memory, raising single-trial success over twelve scenarios, eight of them new but structurally similar, from 22% for planner without memory to 80%. Storage is only half of reuse: retriever must select the record, and recipient must assign it the right role. How long memory lives also limits what it can show. With the foundation policy of Zeva (Chen et al., 2026a) fixed, removing its interaction memory lowers success by 1020 percentage points on five real ChemLab-Evo tasks, but the store is cleared before each episode, so the benefit is adaptation across retries within an episode. Reusing skills and code. one-off recovery becomes reusable skill only when it is detached from the incident that produced it, with an implementation, callable interface, and stated conditions and effects that let planner place it in new sequence. Implementations come from demonstrations in LOTUS (Wan et al., 2024) and Uni-Skill (Xie et al., 2026b), and from person when the library cannot carry out the plan 25 PhysicalRSI 3 / Mechanisms toward Physical RSI in HaLP (Parakh et al., 2024). The robots own execution supplies them in MobiAgent (Liu et al., 2026a) and ReSYNC (Li et al., 2026a). MobiAgent clusters verified deployment rollouts into atomic skills and raises real success on an Astribot S1 from 32.5% to 57.5%, and ReSYNC learns recovery policies together with the symbolic predicates and operators that let planner compose them. Code-writing agents often call two artifacts skills: callable routine and guidance for constructing one. LRLL (Tziafas and Kasaei, 2024) distills simulated instructionprogram pairs into callable Python APIs under curriculum. ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026a) retrieves guidance distilled from earlier program repairs when debugging new controller; on three physical tasks whose embodiment and API differ from the simulation source, retrieval reduces the reasoning tokens spent on the real robot, and held-out success is unchanged on one task and improves on two. Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (Wang et al., 2026i) revises symbolic skills and its system prompt during simulated practice, keeps change only after cross-task check, and reaches 95.0% against 75.5% for ASPIRE on held-out initializations of 22 simulated tasks; the frozen system succeeds in all 30 physical trials. Libraries can also be built in advance and frozen, and the clearest results come from passing frozen library to fresh or weaker agents. RATs (Zhang et al., 2026f) distills successful play into code-skill library for simulated LIBERO-PRO tasks. EmbodiedEvo (Li et al., 2026g) keeps code skills and written lessons that raise fresh agents success on unseen layouts of the RoboDojo simulation benchmark (Chen et al., 2026g) from 8.50% to 30.17%, with similar success at 53.0% lower execution cost than the raw interaction history. Its frozen library also raises weaker executor that failed to acquire it by 8.86 percentage points over no experience. PhysRSI-eval (Li et al., 2026j) freezes GPT-6 Astra workspaces after six rounds of revision on six RoboDojo tasks and tests each on five unseen layouts with no further revision; across 12 workspaces, the stored files alone succeed in 25 of 60 tests. Workspaces pooled from the other tasks also bring the first success earlier in three cases, for example from round 14 to round 7 for Claude Opus 5.5 on the Organize Table task. RoboSkill (Xie et al., 2026c) reports real-robot gains on its hard tasks, and Agent as Policy (Jia et al., 2026) shortens execution across repeated real trials. Embodied Turing Machines (Hu et al., 2026b) make every decision in code on simulated bimanual tasks  (Table 11)  . frozen library can also be written from demonstrations rather than practice. In an evaluation of GPT-6-Astra (Cai et al., 2026), the model studies tasks training demonstrations and writes task guidance, motion references, executable helpers, and recovery procedures into package that is frozen before testing and given to every fresh test session. On four simulated humanoid tasks of the SIMPLE benchmark, the package raises success from 70.8% to 90.8% (120 episodes per condition), with gains that depend on how closely the demonstrations cover the test tasks. Studies that vary the retained artifact while holding its user fixed show most clearly what the artifact must encode. ReTrace (Yu et al., 2026a) lets model controlling real Franka arm trace late failure to an earlier decision, test one correction per attempt, and keep supported corrections as text skill. With skills that one model learned in few attempts, second executing model raises plug insertion and ball pouring from 0% to 80% and 100%, respectively, over ten real trials each. In code-transfer study (Kuroki and Tang, 2026), with the coding model, cases, interfaces, and per-session limits held fixed, mean success on nine new tasks in the simulated RoboCasa environment (Nasiriany et al., 2024) is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source programs, and 57.0% with execution-optimized ones: retained artifact helps only if it encodes distinctions that the next synthesizer can exploit. Even correct skill fails if it is called under the wrong conditions, and some systems revise those conditions directly. The runtime selects context, monitors progress, interrupts, routes control to recoveries, and decides when the nominal policy may resume; revising it can change the effective agent while the weights of planner and controller stay fixed. The reported comparisons show that runtime components interact, and most of them are measured in simulation. SHAPER (Wang et al., 2026e) edits textual procedural guidance and Python harness around frozen planner and executor, and on VLABench (Zhang et al., 2025d) the two edits are not additive: the full configuration scores 34.50% against 28.25% for the seed, less than the skill-only and harness-only gains combined.
